title: Is there a pharmacy near here?
goal: Say that something exists with *c'è* and *ci sono*, name places around town, and master prepositions merged with articles.
bekal: say where things are with *sopra*, *sotto*, *dentro*, *accanto a*

dialogs.title: Dialogo — In cerca di una farmacia
dialogs.intro: Budi isn't feeling well and is looking for a pharmacy. Watch the merged words like *nella*, *del*, *sulla* — they're the heart of this unit.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Scusi, c'è una farmacia qui vicino?
lines.id: Excuse me, is there a pharmacy near here?
lines.literal: excuse-me, there-is a pharmacy here near?

lines.speaker: Signora:
lines.text: Sì, ce n'è una nella piazza, davanti alla banca.
lines.id: Yes, there's one in the square, in front of the bank.
lines.literal: yes, there of-it-is one in-the square, in-front to-the bank.

lines.speaker: Signora:
lines.text: No, cinque minuti a piedi. Vada dritto fino al semaforo.
lines.id: No, five minutes on foot. Go straight on to the traffic lights.
lines.literal: no, five minutes on feet. go(formal) straight until to-the traffic-light.

lines.speaker: Signora:
lines.text: Poi a destra. La farmacia è accanto al supermercato.
lines.id: Then right. The pharmacy is next to the supermarket.
lines.literal: then to right. the pharmacy is beside to-the supermarket.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ci sono anche altre farmacie in centro?
lines.id: Are there other pharmacies downtown too?
lines.literal: there are also other pharmacies in center?

lines.speaker: Signora:
lines.text: Ce ne sono tre, ma la domenica sono chiuse quasi tutte.
lines.id: There are three, but on Sundays almost all of them are closed.
lines.literal: there of-them are three, but the Sunday are closed almost all.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: E se è chiusa? Non c'è niente di aperto?
lines.id: And if it's closed? Is there nothing open?
lines.literal: and if is closed? not there-is nothing of open?

lines.speaker: Signora:
lines.text: C'è sempre una farmacia di turno. L'elenco è sulla porta.
lines.id: There's always a pharmacy on duty. The list is on the door.
lines.literal: there-is always a pharmacy of turn. the list is on-the door.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: That's so kind, thanks a lot!

lines.speaker: Signora:
lines.id: Not at all. Get well soon!

notes: **C'è and ci sono are one pair, just like English "there is" and "there are".** *C'è* for one thing, *ci sono* for several. *C'è una farmacia*, *ci sono tre farmacie*. What decides is the thing that follows, not the speaker.
**Don't confuse it with è.** *È una farmacia* means "it's a pharmacy". *C'è una farmacia* means "there's a pharmacy". Dropping the *ci* changes the meaning completely.

**Ce n'è and ce ne sono.** When the thing has already been mentioned, it's replaced by *ne* ("of it/of them"): *Ce n'è una* (there's one), *ce ne sono tre* (there are three). It sounds complicated but it's used all the time — learn those two sentences whole first.
**Merged prepositions.** *A + la* becomes *alla*, *in + la* becomes *nella*, *su + la* becomes *sulla*. This isn't a stylistic choice but a requirement: writing *a la banca* is wrong.
**Vada and guarisca are formal commands.** With strangers, commands use a special form that's unpacked in Unit 16. For now, just recognize what they mean.
**Si figuri** = "don't mention it", a polite reply to thanks. The informal form is *figurati*. It belongs with *prego* and *di niente*.

**Farmacia di turno.** Italian pharmacies take turns opening outside business hours and on holidays, and the rota is posted on the door of every pharmacy. Practical knowledge that can save a Saturday night.
**Quasi tutte** = almost all. *Tutto* agrees in gender and number: *tutto il giorno*, *tutta la notte*, *tutti i giorni*, *tutte le farmacie*.

grammars.title: Prepositions merged with articles
body: Five prepositions must merge. Learn this table once and use it for life.
after: The pattern is very regular: take the preposition, attach the article, drop the letters that collide. *Di + il* → *del*, *in + il* → *nel*, *su + il* → *sul*.
*Con* (with) and *per* (for) do **not** merge in modern Italian: *con il treno*, *per il fine settimana*. The form *col* is still heard but feels old-fashioned.
⚠️ Merging is only required when there actually is an article. *Vado a Roma* stays *a Roma* because city names don't take an article; but *vado al mercato* must merge.

grammars.title: Saying where things are
body: Some location words are followed by *a* or *di*, and that word merges too.

English
Example
rows: tra la banca e il bar

after: The six that attach to *a* or *da* are the ones most often used wrongly. Learn them together with their preposition, just as you learn nouns together with their article.

blocks.text: Watch out for *la libreria*: it's a bookstore, **not** a library. A library is *la biblioteca*. A classic false friend for English speakers.

blocks.title: Ready-made sentences
items: *C'è un bagno qui?* — Is there a restroom here?
*È lontano da qui?* — Is it far from here?
*Quanto tempo ci vuole?* — How long does it take?
*È aperto adesso?* — Is it open now?
*A che ora chiude?* — What time does it close?
